media: Below is a video of someone playing it: the first evening of the season in full (at one point the player zooms all the way in for a low view), then a montage of later evenings (each one shown from its opening and then from just before the sun sets; in one the player brings along a second, older dog), then a harder 'Wolf Moon' replay of the storm evening, ending with the last minute of a night watch.
first_impression: It's an unexpectedly tense and charming herding sim that nails the core fantasy of being a working border collie. The clean low-poly look and Scottish pastoral vibe immediately grab you, though the bird's-eye camera can feel a bit sterile compared to the pretty ground-level vistas. Once the wolves show up and the weather kicks in, it shifts from relaxing stroll to frantic plate-spinning faster than I anticipated.
best_things: The escalation of mechanics across the season - from stubborn rams and lost lambs to flooded bridges and blizzard visibility - keeps each run fresh.
The wolf snatch alerts and rescue dashes create genuine adrenaline without breaking the cozy countryside aesthetic.
The charm system and the ability to command a second veteran dog (Old Fly) add real tactical depth to what could have been a shallow gimmick.

worst_problems.problem: The camera defaults to an almost clinical top-down satellite view, stripping away the gorgeous atmospheric landscapes teased during cutscenes.
worst_problems.suggestion: Give us a dynamic isometric tilt or an adjustable third-person camera toggle during normal gameplay so we can actually see the horizon and sunset while playing.

worst_problems.problem: Sheep pathfinding through narrow gates and bridges gets clunky, leading to awkward bottleneck bunching where sheep grind against fences.
worst_problems.suggestion: Smooth out the flock fluid dynamics around chokepoints and gate posts so sheep naturally funnel instead of clipping and sticking to collision edges.

worst_problems.problem: UI alerts and UI popups (like wolf distance meters and tutorial prompts) stack heavily in the center of the screen, creating visual clutter during high-stress moments.
worst_problems.suggestion: Move the wolf snatch telemetry and timer boxes to the edge of the HUD or integrate them as world-space audio/visual cues.

worst_problems.problem: The trial trial course (Glenbrae Trial) feels overly rigid and punishing compared to the organic open-field herding of the rest of the campaign.
worst_problems.suggestion: Make the gate trigger zones slightly more forgiving and provide clearer ground-painted drift lines to guide turns.

worst_problems.problem: The flat grass texture and repetitive ground details in standard daytime maps look a bit stark and mobile-game-ish before the fog or snow sets in.
worst_problems.suggestion: Add more procedural foliage tufts, flowers, wind ripples, and soil variation across the meadow turf.

boredom_points: Trudging at walking pace behind a slow-moving cluster on long straight dirt paths when no wolves are near (e.g. 08:18 - 08:30).
Waiting out the last thirty seconds of the Night Watch level when all wolves have already backed off (16:00 - 16:23).
confusions: At first glance, understanding whether 'creep' or 'bark' is better against stubborn sheep like Old Angus until the text tutorial explicitly clarifies it.
How wolf aggro works across water - it isn't immediately obvious whether wolves can swim or ford the stream until they cross over.
wish_list: A free-roam endless practice paddock or custom weather sandbox mode.
More shepherd whistled commands and customizable dog coats.
A playable third-person camera mode behind Pip.
one_line_review: Equal parts soothing pastoral simulator and nerve-shredding wolf thriller - an absolute gem of an indie herding game.
